message.content:
Here are some of the most popular and highly regarded sushi restaurants in Tokyo—ranging from Michelin‑starred establishments to well‑known local favorites:

| Restaurant | Location | Highlights | Notes |
|------------|----------|------------|-------|
| **Sukiyabashi Jiro** | Ginza (original) & Roppongi (new) | Legendary chef Jiro Ono, 3 Michelin stars, meticulous nigiri | Very expensive; reservations required months in advance. |
| **Sushi Saito** | Minato | 3 Michelin stars, intimate 10‑seat setting, exceptional omakase | Extremely hard to book; often requires a reservation through a concierge or a Japanese friend. |
| **Sushi Yoshitake** | Ginza | 3 Michelin stars, refined omakase, seasonal ingredients | Reservations needed; offers a tasting menu with a focus on subtle flavors. |
| **Sushi Dai** | Tsukiji Outer Market | Famous for fresh tuna, long lines, casual vibe | No reservations; best to arrive early (before 8 am). |
| **Sushi Daiwa** | Tsukiji Outer Market | Similar to Sushi Dai but slightly less crowded | Great for a quick, high‑quality sushi experience. |
| **Sushi Kyubey** | Ginza | 2 Michelin stars, classic Edo‑style sushi, friendly staff | Reservations recommended; offers both lunch and dinner menus. |
| **Sushi Masuda** | Ginza | 2 Michelin stars, known for its “sashimi” style and creative rolls | Reservations needed; offers a la carte options. |
| **Sushi Iwa** | Shinjuku | 1 Michelin star, small intimate setting, excellent for beginners | Reservations recommended; offers a set menu. |
| **Sushi Tsubaki** | Shibuya | 1 Michelin star, modern take on traditional sushi | Reservations recommended; offers a tasting menu. |
| **Sushi Kanda** | Minato | 3 Michelin stars, renowned for its precision and artistry | Reservations required; offers a multi‑course omakase. |
| **Sushi Saito** | Minato | 3 Michelin stars, intimate 10‑seat setting, exceptional omakase | Extremely hard to book; often requires a reservation through a concierge or a Japanese friend. |
| **Sushi Noda** | Shinjuku | 1 Michelin star, known for its fresh fish and friendly service | Reservations recommended; offers a set menu. |
| **Sushi Shun** | Ginza | 1 Michelin star, elegant setting, seasonal omakase | Reservations recommended; offers a tasting menu. |
| **Sushi Iwa** | Shinjuku | 1 Michelin star, small intimate setting, excellent for beginners | Reservations recommended; offers a set menu. |
| **Sushi Tsubaki** | Shibuya | 1 Michelin star, modern take on traditional sushi | Reservations recommended; offers a tasting menu. |
| **Sushi Kanda** | Minato | 3 Michelin stars, renowned for its precision and artistry | Reservations required; offers a multi‑course omakase. |

### Tips for Visiting

1. **Reservations** – For Michelin‑starred spots, book at least 2–3 months ahead. Many require a Japanese phone number or a concierge service.
2. **Dress Code** – Some upscale restaurants have a dress code; it’s best to wear smart casual attire.
3. **Payment** – Credit cards are accepted at most high‑end places, but some smaller shops may only take cash.
4. **Tipping** – Not customary in Japan; excellent service is expected as part of the dining experience.

Enjoy your sushi adventure in Tokyo!
